title: The milkmaid's vocation
hook: Luther said a milkmaid's work pleases God as much as a monk's

segments.voice: Yesterday, Wesley's three rules for money: earn honestly, save by cutting waste, and then give. Your line was give all you can. Did the amount you found make it out the door? Day one thousand two hundred fourteen.

Before dawn, in a cold barn, a young woman sits on a stool with her cheek against a cow's warm side, and the milk rings into the pail. Up the hill, in a monastery, a monk is already at prayer in the chapel. Ask the village which of the two is doing holy work, and the answer comes fast. Martin Luther gave a different answer, and it startled people. Christians still repeat a saying credited to him: the milkmaid's work, done in faith, pleases God as much as the monk's. Today's word: vocation.

A vocation is a calling. In the world Luther grew up in, the word had come to belong to one kind of life: priests, monks and nuns. They had a calling. Everyone else simply had a job. Luther pushed back hard. He argued that God calls the farmer, the parent, the shoemaker and the servant girl just as truly, and that their work serves God by serving neighbors. The baby gets fed. The town has shoes. The bread arrives. He leaned on Paul's advice to the Corinthians: "Let every man abide in the same calling wherein he was called." Paul is saying your ordinary station is where faith gets lived, right where you stand. Paul says it another way in Colossians, writing to people who were servants: "And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men." Notice who that was written to. Not preachers. People doing someone else's chores. Their work, done heartily, is done for the Lord. This idea took root in the churches that came from Luther, and it isn't only theirs. Catholic teaching today also speaks of the vocation of lay people, and of work as a share in God's own work. Luther, a former monk himself, never stopped praying. What he argued against was the idea that a monk's vows earned more with God than a farmer's faith. He refused a ladder, with spiritual jobs at the top and the barn at the bottom. Diapers, spreadsheets, a cash register: in this view, they can be a calling too.
screen: `DO IT HEARTILY, AS TO THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see your work as a calling. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the most ordinary task waiting for you today: the email, the dishes, the shift, the homework, the commute. Now trace it outward. Who does it serve? Someone eats, someone gets paid, someone's day gets a little easier. Follow it until you can picture one actual person on the other end. Then picture doing that task heartily, for them. If you pray, you can offer that task to God before you begin it. The bell holds the time.
Vocation. A calling. In Luther's teaching, not only for priests and monks, but for anyone whose ordinary work serves a neighbor.
Your line: every job is holy. Today, do your most ordinary task heartily, and think once of the person it serves. Day one thousand two hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Lutheran and other Protestant churches teach the doctrine of vocation, that ordinary work and family life are callings from God; Catholic teaching also speaks of the vocation of lay people in the world, and some churches bless workers and their tools.

fork.setup: you're the milkmaid. a traveling preacher tells you the monk's prayers please God more than your milking. what does Luther say?
options: he's right; leave the barn for the convent.

fork.reveal: Luther refused the ladder of holy jobs. the barn can be a calling as much as the chapel, because the work serves a neighbor.

original.note: Greek, 1 Corinthians 7:20: a calling, the word Paul uses for where a person was called.

trapdoor: what you thought: a vocation is a job for priests and nuns.
what it means: a calling. Luther taught that ordinary work serving a neighbor is a calling too.
what a scholar hears: Paul's word in 1 Corinthians 7:20 is klesis, a calling. in the same chapter, the call comes to people right where they already are.

notes: The milkmaid saying is widely credited to Luther, but its exact source and wording are uncertain (it may be a later summary of his teaching); the script says 'a saying credited to him'. Confirm the hedge.
'In the world Luther grew up in, the word had come to belong to one kind of life' summarizes the medieval usage of vocatio for religious life; confirm.
Trapdoor: klesis in 1 Corinthians 7:17–24, where Paul tells people to remain in the condition in which they were called; confirm the gloss.
Catechism references for lay vocation (898–900) and work as participation in creation (2427) given from memory; confirm numbers.

Audit pass: 'neither side throws out the monk' overstated Luther's position (he left the monastery, married, and attacked monastic vows as meritorious in On Monastic Vows, 1521). Replaced with: Luther, a former monk, kept praying, but argued a monk's vows earned no more with God than a farmer's faith. Confirm.
Colossians 3:22–23 is addressed to servants ('Servants, obey in all things your masters'); the script notes this without comment on slavery. A Keeper may want a note.
